questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A digest sent alongside the message it describes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a digest travelling with its message proves
questions.stem: A field survey brief says each uploaded sighting record carries a digest of the record next to the record itself. Which statement about that digest is correct?

options.text: Anyone who has the record can recompute the digest, so the pair shows the record was not altered
Only the tablet that produced the record can recompute the digest, so the pair proves which device sent it
options.misconception: assumes computing a digest requires a secret key

options.text: The digest hides the contents of the record from anyone who can see the file
options.misconception: treats a digest as if it concealed the record

options.text: The digest can be used to recover the original record when the survey laptop is lost
options.misconception: believes a digest can be reversed into the record

questions.explanation: A digest is computable by anyone from the same input, so sending it beside the record lets the receiver detect a change without proving anything about the sender. The tempting options claim secrecy, origin evidence or reversibility.
questions.hint: Nothing secret is needed to compute a digest.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A per-record random value
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a per-record random value changes for identical records
questions.stem: A survey brief says each stored record carries its own random value. Two rows in the store contain identical text. What does the random value achieve for those two rows?

options.text: It hides the text of both rows from anyone who can read the store
options.misconception: treats the random value as encryption of the row

options.text: It makes the stored digests for the two rows differ, so equal records cannot be spotted by matching digests
It proves that both rows were entered by the same observer
options.misconception: claims the random value carries identity evidence

options.text: It guarantees that the two rows came from different field sites
options.misconception: believes a random value records where data came from

questions.explanation: A random value that differs per record makes the stored digests of identical records differ, so matching digests reveal nothing. The tempting options claim secrecy, proof of authorship or a record of where the data was collected.
questions.hint: Ask what becomes different between two equal records.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A secret input kept outside the store
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a secret held outside the store adds to a sign-in check
questions.stem: A survey brief says the field tablets store only a hash of each collector's pass phrase, while a second secret lives on the office server and is added only when a sign-in is checked. Explain what that second secret adds.

answer.exemplar: The server-held secret means a stolen tablet full of stored hashes cannot be attacked offline, because each guess needs the extra secret that never left the office. It also means an attacker who reaches only the store still cannot compute the expected value, although the office server becomes the piece that must be protected and kept available.

questions.explanation: The secret on the server stops a copied store from being enough to mount an offline guessing attack. The tempting wrong idea is that hashing alone is sufficient, or that keeping the secret outside the store removes the need to protect the server.
questions.hint: Ask what an attacker with only the tablet can test.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY

questions.stem: A survey brief stores one 32-byte verifier value for each of the 240 collectors on the team. How many kilobytes of storage do those values occupy?
questions.explanation: Two hundred and forty values of 32 bytes each take 7680 bytes, which is 7.5 kilobytes at 1024 bytes to the kilobyte. The tempting answer treats a kilobyte as 1000 bytes and gives 7.68.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Choosing a work setting
questions.learningObjective: Choose and justify a work setting for a sign-in check

stimulus.body: A survey brief says the sign-in check for the field tablet is deliberately slow so that guessing many pass phrases on stolen hardware becomes expensive. The brief records that the same hardware must still finish each check in a fraction of a second.

questions.stem: Given the brief, which setting is the team choosing and why?

options.text: A low work setting, because it keeps every check inside a fraction of a second on the tablet
options.misconception: ignores that speed is what an offline attacker wants

options.text: A high work setting, because it guarantees that no observer can time the check
options.misconception: claims a work setting hides timing information

options.text: A high work setting, because making each guess expensive slows down an offline attack
A low work setting, because stored values cannot be attacked without the server secret
options.misconception: assumes the stored value alone cannot be attacked

questions.explanation: A high work setting multiplies the cost of each guess, which is what makes a stolen store of stored values unattractive. The tempting options confuse the checker's speed with the attacker's difficulty, and one wrongly credits the server secret with covering every case.
questions.hint: Ask what the attacker pays for each guess.

questions.topic: What the storage combination does and leaves

questions.stem: A brief describes what is kept with each stored credential: a random value that is public, and a digest computed over that value together with the pass phrase. Which statement is correct about the stored combination?

options.text: It proves the pass phrase is correct, but it cannot stop two records sharing a value
options.misconception: claims the combination proves correctness to anyone reading it

options.text: It hides the pass phrase completely, but it cannot detect a changed record
options.misconception: treats the combination as encryption of the pass phrase

options.text: It shows when the pass phrase was set, but it cannot resist guessing
options.misconception: believes the combination records a timestamp

options.text: It makes each stored value unique per record, but it cannot tell you who chose the pass phrase

questions.explanation: Mixing a per-record random value into the digest makes each stored value unique, while the combination still says nothing about who chose the phrase. The tempting options claim proof of correctness, secrecy or a timestamp, none of which the stored pair provides.
questions.hint: Ask what two equal pass phrases produce.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a key derivation is for
questions.learningObjective: State the purpose a key derivation serves in a key hierarchy
questions.stem: A field office brief says the station derives separate working keys from one master secret, one for the tablets and one for the archive. What is a key derivation for in this design?

options.text: To turn one master secret into purpose-specific keys so a leak in one place does not expose the other
To make the master secret longer so that it takes more characters to guess
options.misconception: believes derivation only lengthens a secret

options.text: To encrypt the archive so that the tablets could not read it
options.misconception: confuses derivation with encryption of stored data

options.text: To let each collector choose a key that the office never learns
options.misconception: describes agreement rather than derivation

questions.explanation: Derivation produces separate, purpose-bound keys from one root secret, so a weakness in one area does not spread to the others. The tempting options reduce derivation to length, encryption or key agreement, none of which is its job.
questions.hint: Ask what changes when one derived key leaks.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Telling three similar functions apart
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish hashing, keyed authentication and derivation by their job
questions.stem: A brief mentions three functions in one paragraph: one that reduces a pass phrase to a stored value, one that authenticates a message with a key, and one that stretches a short input into a long key. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Hashing authenticates a message with a key, keyed authentication reduces a pass phrase, and derivation stretches
options.misconception: swaps the roles of hashing and keyed authentication

options.text: Hashing reduces a pass phrase, keyed authentication uses a key, and derivation stretches an input
Hashing reduces a pass phrase, keyed authentication stretches an input, and derivation authenticates messages
options.misconception: swaps the roles of derivation and keyed authentication

options.text: All three do the same job and differ only in the length of their output
options.misconception: claims the three functions are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Hashing reduces input to a fixed value, keyed authentication checks a message using a key, and derivation stretches a short input into key material. The tempting options swap the roles of the three functions or treat them as one thing in three sizes.
questions.hint: Ask which one needs a key and which one stretches.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A digest sent alongside the message it describes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a digest sent with a message detects and misses
questions.stem: A survey brief has each tablet send a record together with a digest of that record, and the office recomputes the digest to decide whether to accept it. Explain what this detects and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: Recomputing the digest on arrival shows whether the bytes received are the bytes that were sent, so a corrupted or altered upload is caught and can be requested again. It does not show that the record came from a genuine tablet, because the digest is computed without any secret and anyone can produce a matching one.

questions.explanation: The digest catches corruption and alteration in transit, but with no secret involved it cannot establish who sent the record. The tempting wrong idea treats recomputation as an authenticity check.
questions.hint: Ask what a digest computed without a secret can prove.

questions.topic: A secret input kept outside the store

options.text: The server can decrypt the survey records that the tablets have collected
options.misconception: claims the secret gives the server the record contents

options.text: The tablets no longer need to store anything at all about the collectors
options.misconception: believes the secret removes the need for stored values

options.text: Stolen tablets yield nothing that can be attacked without also reaching the server
Sign-in checks become fast enough to run on the oldest field hardware
options.misconception: claims a server secret speeds up the check

questions.explanation: Holding the secret on the server means a copied tablet yields stored values that cannot be tested for guesses on their own. The tempting options invent decryption, the removal of stored values or a speed-up, none of which follows from the arrangement.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a sign-in check has to be able to do
questions.learningObjective: State the requirement that makes a sign-in check resist bulk guessing
questions.stem: A brief requires a sign-in check to do two things: confirm the supplied pass phrase matches the stored value, and resist being run many times against stolen stored values. Which option states the second requirement correctly?

options.text: The check must return the pass phrase itself, so the office can confirm what the collector typed
options.misconception: requires the office to hold the pass phrase

options.text: The check must work without any stored value, so a collector can sign in on a new tablet
options.misconception: demands a check with nothing to compare against

options.text: The check must finish in under a millisecond, so that a collector is never kept waiting
options.misconception: treats speed as the requirement

options.text: The check must be hard to run in bulk, so that each guess against a stolen value is expensive

questions.explanation: Resistance to bulk guessing comes from making each individual check costly, so thousands of attempts take correspondingly long. The tempting options ask the check to reveal the phrase, to work without a stored value or to be fast, none of which resists guessing.
questions.hint: Ask what an attacker pays per attempt.

questions.topic: Choosing a work setting
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reasoning behind adjusting the work setting
questions.stem: Under the survey guidance the sign-in check runs with a deliberately large amount of work, and the office raises it whenever the field hardware gets faster. Which statement best describes the reasoning?

options.text: The work setting controls the cost of one guess, so raising it raises the cost of an offline attack
The work setting sets the length of the stored value, so raising it stores more bytes
options.misconception: believes the work setting controls stored value length

options.text: The work setting decides how long a pass phrase may be, so raising it rejects shorter ones
options.misconception: believes the work setting enforces a length rule

options.text: The work setting chooses the algorithm, so raising it selects a stronger hash function
options.misconception: believes the work setting selects the algorithm

questions.explanation: The work setting multiplies the effort required for each guess, so raising it raises the cost of an offline attack in proportion. The tempting options confuse it with value length, pass phrase rules or algorithm choice.

options.text: The stored value can be read back as the original pass phrase by the office
options.misconception: assumes the stored value reveals the pass phrase

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a key derivation is for
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a derived key beats using the root secret directly
questions.stem: A survey brief derives a separate working key for the archive from one master secret. Explain why deriving a separate key is better than using the master secret directly for the archive.

answer.exemplar: If the archive key is derived, then a weakness found in the archive code exposes only that derived key, while the master secret and the tablet key stay untouched. Using the master secret directly for both purposes means any failure in one place reveals material that also protects the other, and the damage compounds.

questions.explanation: Derivation isolates each purpose so a failure in one area cannot reach the root secret. The tempting wrong idea is that one secret is simpler and therefore safer, ignoring how exposure spreads.
questions.hint: Ask which key is lost when the archive is breached.

options.text: Evidence that the digest came from a tablet holding that key, rather than being made by anyone
The ability to read the observation without having the uploaded bytes
options.misconception: claims the signature reveals the content

options.text: A guarantee that the uploaded bytes were never changed after the tablet signed them
options.misconception: claims the signature covers later changes

questions.explanation: Signing the digest binds it to the tablet that holds the key, which the plain digest alone could never show. The tempting options claim the signature proves location, reveals content or protects the bytes from later changes.
questions.hint: Ask what the signature proves that the bare digest cannot.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A per-record random value
questions.learningObjective: Spot evidence that one random value was reused across records
questions.stem: Every record in the survey store holds a random value and a digest over that value and the pass phrase. Which observation would show the same random value reused across records?

options.text: Two records with identical content show different stored digests
options.misconception: describes correct per-record behaviour

options.text: Every record shows a stored digest of the same fixed length
options.misconception: reads a fixed length as evidence of reuse

options.text: Two records with identical content show the same stored digest
Every record shows a stored digest that differs from the content it describes
options.misconception: reads digest mismatch as evidence of reuse

questions.explanation: If one value were reused, equal content would produce equal stored digests, which is the visible signal. The tempting observations describe correct behaviour or read fixed lengths and digest differences as evidence of reuse.
questions.hint: Ask what equal content would produce if the value were shared.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A secret input kept outside the store
questions.learningObjective: Describe the paired effects of a server-held secret
questions.stem: A brief keeps a second secret on the office server and mixes it into each sign-in check. Which pair of outcomes describes the effect of that arrangement?

options.text: Stored values can be attacked offline, but the office server holds no useful material
options.misconception: claims the server secret is useless

options.text: Collectors can sign in with no server at all, and the office learns nothing new
options.misconception: claims the check no longer needs the server

options.text: The server can decrypt the stored values, and collectors can recover their pass phrases
options.misconception: claims the arrangement enables decryption and recovery

options.text: Stored values cannot be attacked offline, but the office server becomes critical to every sign-in

questions.explanation: Moving a secret off the tablet blocks offline guessing but makes the server part of every sign-in and a valuable target. The tempting options claim the opposite effects, or invent decryption and recovery of pass phrases.
questions.hint: Ask what has been traded away by moving the secret.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a sign-in check has to be able to do
questions.learningObjective: Select the check that meets the field and stolen-value requirements
questions.stem: A survey brief says the sign-in check must work when the collector is on poor signal and must not be defeated by a copy of the stored values. Which check fits both requirements?

options.text: A check that sends the stored value to the tablet for the tablet to compare locally
options.misconception: describes handing stored values to the tablet

options.text: A check that asks the collector a secret question they answered in training
options.misconception: relies on shared knowledge instead of a stored value

options.text: A check that sends the pass phrase to the office for a plain comparison
options.misconception: requires sending the pass phrase in the clear

options.text: A check that compares a recomputed value with a stored one and is deliberately expensive to run

questions.explanation: Only a check that recomputes and compares locally on the tablet avoids depending on the network, and making it expensive keeps copied stored values from being useful. The tempting options need the network, rely on shared knowledge, or send the pass phrase in the clear.
questions.hint: Ask which option needs no network and no copied store.
